readerTitle: The free newspaper that was never really about the news
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Metro, 1995년 스톡홀름 무료 신문) + 실제 관찰 (무료 앱과 웹사이트의 광고 모델) + 가상 적용 (택배 차량 광고)
insight: 광고 모델에서 회사가 실제로 만들고 파는 것은 콘텐츠가 아니라 '설명할 수 있는 특정 청중의 주의'다. 청중의 크기보다 광고주가 그 청중을 그려 볼 수 있는지가 값을 정한다.
misconception: 사용자나 방문자가 많으면 광고 수익은 저절로 따라오고, 광고는 원래 하던 일에 얹는 공짜 부수입이다.

sources.text: Metro International, company history (Metro launched in Stockholm in 1995, distributed free on public transport, funded by advertising)
무료 앱·웹사이트 광고 모델과 스마트폰 보급 이후 무료 신문의 축소는 일반적 업계 관찰
택배 차량 광고 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Metro가 1995년 2월 스톡홀름 지하철에서 무료로 창간되었고 수입을 광고에만 의존했다는 점을 Metro International 자료로 다시 확인하세요.
'spread to cities around the world'는 Metro가 여러 나라로 확장했다는 일반적 사실에 근거합니다. 정확한 국가 수는 자료마다 달라 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.
'짧은 기사로 출퇴근 중 다 읽을 수 있게 만들었다'는 Metro의 편집 콘셉트 설명입니다. 회사가 쓴 구체적인 분 단위 문구는 확인 전이라 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
스마트폰 보급 뒤 여러 도시의 무료 신문이 줄거나 폐간했다는 내용은 일반적 관찰로만 적었습니다. 특정 신문의 폐간 연도는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The free newspaper that was never really about the news
body: In 1995, commuters in Stockholm started picking up a new daily paper on the subway. It was free. Every copy, every day.
Readers paid nothing. Yet the paper had a working business model, and it spread to cities around the world.

image.label: Commuters on a subway platform reading the same free newspaper
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 아침 지하철 승강장에서 출근하는 사람들이 모두 같은 무료 신문을 펼쳐 읽는 장면. 신문 1면에 "FREE"라는 큰 글자만 보이게. 실제 신문 제호나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your paper is free. Ads pay all the bills.
body: You're launching a free daily paper in a big city. Printing and staff are paid for only by advertisers.
Which plan makes your paper most valuable to the people paying for it?

options.text: Print as many copies as possible and drop them all over the city
options.feedback: Size matters to advertisers. But copies left in random places reach people nobody can describe, and many go unread, so each copy is worth less.

options.text: Hand it out at busy stations in the morning rush, with stories short enough to finish before your stop
options.feedback: You trade some size for an audience advertisers can picture: working commuters, reading at the same hour every day. That predictability is what they pay for.

options.text: Charge a small price so readers value the paper more
options.feedback: Paying readers may read more closely, but far fewer will pick it up. You shrink the very crowd your advertisers are paying to reach.

cards.title: What Metro actually sold
body: Metro was handed out free on public transport and written in short pieces. All its money came from advertising.

Its real product wasn't the news. It was a large, predictable crowd of working city commuters, reading at the same time every weekday. An advertiser could picture exactly who would see the ad, and when.
The news was what gathered the crowd. The crowd was what Metro sold.

cards.title: Advertising as a business model
body: **Advertising** as a business model means you give people something they want, often for free, and charge a third party to put a message in front of them.
So you have two kinds of customer. The audience pays with attention. The advertiser pays with money. The second one keeps the lights on, but only as long as the first one keeps showing up.

image.label: Triangle: business, audience and advertiser
image.brief: 삼각형 다이어그램. 위쪽 꼭짓점 "Your business", 왼쪽 "Audience", 오른쪽 "Advertiser". 비즈니스에서 청중으로 "Free content" 화살표, 청중에서 비즈니스로 "Attention" 화살표, 광고주에서 비즈니스로 "Money" 화살표. 돈 화살표를 가장 굵게.

cards.title: What advertisers are really paying for
body: An ad buyer is weighing three things:
list: **Reach:** how many people see the message
**Who they are:** an audience the advertiser can describe and wants to sell to
**Attention:** whether people notice the ad, in a place and moment that fits
cards.callout: A smaller audience that advertisers can picture often earns more per person than a huge crowd they can't describe.

cards.title: Free apps run on the same deal.
body: Many free apps and websites work like Metro. Users pay with their time. Advertisers pay to reach them.
Software adds a twist: it can report who saw an ad and who clicked. That makes each view easier to price. It also adds pressure to collect more data about users.
Because a single view earns very little, digital ad businesses usually need either a very large audience or a very specific one.

cards.title: Attention is borrowed, not owned.
body: Every ad uses up some of the attention your audience came for. Add too many, and people drift away. Then the advertisers follow them.
Your paying customer is the advertiser, so decisions tend to tilt toward what advertisers want. That can slowly wear down the trust that gathered the audience.
And attention moves. Once smartphones gave commuters something else to look at, free papers in many cities shrank or closed.

cards.title: Now it's a delivery fleet.
body: You run a regional parcel delivery company. Your 60 vans drive the same city routes every day.
A local car dealer offers a monthly fee to wrap your vans in its ads. What do you do first?

image.label: Delivery vans on a city street, one wrapped in a blank ad panel
image.brief: 도시 거리를 달리는 똑같은 택배 밴 세 대. 그중 한 대 옆면에 빈 광고판 모양의 랩핑이 있고 물음표가 떠 있음. 실제 택배사나 자동차 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

options.text: Accept. The vans drive anyway, so it's pure extra income
options.feedback: Easy money, but you'd take the dealer's price without knowing what your routes are worth. You'd also give up your vans as your own billboard.

options.text: Work out which streets the vans pass and how many people see them, price from that, and keep your own name visible
options.feedback: Fixed routes through busy areas are a predictable audience, and that is what advertisers pay for. Pricing on it earns more without hiding who delivers the parcels.

options.text: Decline. Ads would make the company look cheap
options.feedback: This protects your brand, but it leaves money on the table. A tasteful, limited deal could do both.

cards.title: In advertising, the audience is what you build and what you sell.
body: The free thing gathers people. The money comes from someone who wants to reach them. So the value depends on how clearly you can describe that audience and how carefully you protect its trust.
**Try it today:** list the people who already gather around your business: shoppers, email readers, people who pass your vans. Describe them in one sentence an advertiser would pay for.
